  caller one loop away from a core kept busy by its own wakes.
- **A `cancel` the caller must choose to call.** Every site that gives up its own handle would have
  to remember it, and a registration on the drain holds its handle inside a closure that only a drop
  can reach.
- **Collecting every wake a task delivers to itself, the asked-for one too.** It would change what a
  registration against a drain that has already begun leaves behind, and the idle cost needs none of
  that changed.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/one-permission-per-drive`](concurrency.md#concurrency-one-permission-per-drive), [`concurrency/a-wake-never-moves-a-task`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-wake-never-moves-a-task), [`concurrency/the-parking-contract`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-parking-contract).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-a-cancelled-drive-never-parks-again"></a>

## A cancellation ends the drive: torn down where it parked, or told once and answered

`rule:concurrency/a-cancelled-drive-never-parks-again`

A cancellation ends the drive. The drive adds nothing to the cancellation model and inherits it
whole, and both of the scheduler's two answers stop the loop.

The ordinary one is a teardown, and the drive never returns from it. A parked coroutine whose stack
may be unwound is dropped where it stands, and the unwind drops the future with it — closing the
connection through the host language's own drops, and running no Novis frame.

The other is a resume. A stack standing on a helper frame cannot be unwound, so the scheduler tells
it once, on the way back in; there the loop stops and the drive answers nothing. Parking again would
wait on a wake that is not coming, which is a wedged coroutine rather than a slow one, and going on
would serve a request the client is no longer attached to.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/one-future-per-connection`](concurrency.md#concurrency-one-future-per-connection), [`concurrency/a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-drain-closes-a-connection-cleanly).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-the-park-route-is-chosen-once"></a>

## Where a drive parks is decided once when it starts, and off a core it blocks the thread

`rule:concurrency/the-park-route-is-chosen-once`

Where a drive parks is decided once, when it starts, because a task never migrates and so the answer
cannot change underneath it. There are three routes and no fourth.

On a core with a reactor — the server — a park suspends the task, and the wake is the installed
permission. On a core with no reactor, which is a scheduler-only test, there is nothing to arrange a
wake with, so the drive yields to the back of the run queue and polls again: spinning through the run
queue is deliberate, because a park nothing can end is a wedge. Off a core entirely — a `nvs run`
program, a unit test — the thread itself parks and is unparked.

Blocking the thread is right in that last case for the reason every off-core wait already gives:
there is no coroutine to suspend and no neighbour to starve, so blocking starves nobody. On a core it
would be precisely wrong.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/one-future-per-connection`](concurrency.md#concurrency-one-future-per-connection), [`concurrency/a-waker-is-one-permission-to-poll`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-waker-is-one-permission-to-poll).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-the-parking-contract"></a>

## A task registers before it suspends, treats a wake as a hint, and leaves the reactor holding nothing when it ends

`rule:concurrency/the-parking-contract`

Five rules govern a task that waits on I/O, and the first two are ordering rules a reader will
otherwise get backwards.

1. **Register, then suspend.** A task tells the reactor what it is waiting for, keyed by its own task
   id, and only afterwards parks. The reverse order is a lost wakeup: readiness arriving in the gap
   has nothing registered to record it against.
2. **A wake is a hint, not a promise.** A woken task re-tries its syscall and parks again on another
   `WouldBlock`. Spurious wakes are ordinary — a level-triggered poller reports a socket another read
   already drained, and a wake can race a task that finished — so waking an unknown id answers
   `false` rather than raising a fault.
3. **Deregister when the task ends.** Every registration under that id is dropped when the task is
   retired. A registration that outlives its request is the growth with total traffic that
   [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority) calls a leak rather than a trade-off.
4. **The reactor blocks only when the run queue is empty and something is parked.** With work ready it
   is polled with a zero timeout, so readiness is collected without giving up the core. A task that
   uses up its time slice is parked the same way: it wakes itself and then parks, so the core polls
   the reactor before that task runs again, and a task that never waits cannot keep a ready
   connection or an expired timer from its turn. There is no fourth state.
5. **One reactor per worker**, not shared. A descriptor a request owns is registered with, and woken
   by, that request's own core — which is what keeps refcounts non-atomic.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/the-reactor-reports-readiness`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-reactor-reports-readiness), [`concurrency/try-the-syscall-then-park`](concurrency.md#concurrency-try-the-syscall-then-park), [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-try-the-syscall-then-park"></a>

## A stream issues the syscall first and parks only on `WouldBlock`, so a warm socket pays nothing

`rule:concurrency/try-the-syscall-then-park`

A read is: issue the syscall; on success return; on `WouldBlock` register, suspend, and loop.
Optimistic, not pessimistic, and the order is deliberate.

The costs are not symmetric. A syscall that succeeds is one `recv` and nothing else. A syscall that
returns `WouldBlock` is one failed `recv` — tens of nanoseconds, with no ready-list work in the
kernel. Registering interest is an `epoll_ctl` or an AFD submission, which is the microsecond class
and the expensive half, and the suspension is one stack switch each way. Polling before reading would
pay the microsecond-class registration on **every** read, including the ones that would have
succeeded — and those are the common case, because the first read of an accepted connection almost
always finds the request bytes already buffered: they arrived with the connection.

A registration is kept while the task holds the stream rather than torn down per park, so a stream
that parks repeatedly pays a modification and not a creation.

**A stream keeps a readiness bit, as tokio does, so the syscall is tried only when it might
succeed.** A `WouldBlock` clears the bit. Any readiness event the reactor reports for the task the
stream is registered under sets it again. The reactor's tokens are task ids, so the bit is the
reactor's per-task event count, taken at the `WouldBlock` and compared on the next read. A poll that
finds the bit clear files its deadline and arms exactly as a `WouldBlock` would, and answers
`Pending` with no syscall. The first read after registration, a read after any change of
registration and a read off a core always try the syscall. An event on another descriptor of the
same task sets the bit too, which costs one extra failed `recv` and never a missed one.

What it spends: four bytes per registered task in the reactor, and four per stream.

**Declined:**
- **A bit set by the event for the descriptor itself.** The token would have to name the stream,
  which is a second table beside the task ids for one failed `recv` saved per shared wake.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/the-parking-contract`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-parking-contract), [`concurrency/a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-the-reactor-reports-readiness"></a>

## The reactor reports readiness on every platform, Windows included, so a stream is written once

`rule:concurrency/the-reactor-reports-readiness`

The reactor reports **readiness**, never completion, on every platform: epoll on Linux, kqueue on the
BSDs and macOS, and on Windows a poll of `\Device\Afd` through the completion port, which turns it
into a readiness source. One contract, three back ends, and the stream code above it is written once.

That choice is the reason there is one stream implementation rather than two.

The readiness layer is a poller and not an async runtime: no executor, no task type, no futures. The
runtime brings its own scheduler ([`concurrency/the-parking-contract`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-parking-contract)), and nothing
attacker-controlled reaches a registration, which carries a descriptor and an interest set and no
parsed input at all.

**Declined:**
- **Completion semantics on Windows.** It is the native contract there and faster at very high
  connection counts, but a completion-based read owns its buffer across a suspension and a
  readiness-based one does not. Every stream and every helper that reads one would exist twice, and
  the copy that gets less traffic would be on a first-class platform.
- **Hand-written epoll, kqueue and AFD back ends.** Three `unsafe` FFI layers with nothing specific to
  this runtime in any of them, against a pure-Rust poller whose whole surface is exactly this. What is
  specific is the parking contract above it.
- **An async runtime such as `tokio`.** Its value is an executor and a task model, and the runtime has
  its own, in which a stackful coroutine suspends from *inside a helper*, which a future cannot.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/the-parking-contract`](concurrency.md#concurrency-the-parking-contract), [`concurrency/try-the-syscall-then-park`](concurrency.md#concurrency-try-the-syscall-then-park).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream"></a>

## A parking stream is a plain `Read` and `Write`, so nothing up the call chain is coloured

`rule:concurrency/a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream`

A parking socket implements nothing but `std::io::Read` and `std::io::Write`. Its signature says
nothing about suspension, and no caller up the chain is marked: a helper reads it with the same call
it would use on a blocking socket, and an unmodified protocol implementation — a TLS session, a
sans-IO codec — drives it without knowing what it is.

There is no colour, anywhere. No `await`, no async member, and no second spelling of any `Core` member
that touches I/O. The suspension route travels in the context rather than in the type, which is
precisely what makes that possible.

What it costs is that a stack is the unit of concurrency
([`concurrency/a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled)): a task is about a megabyte of address
space rather than the hundred bytes a stackless future would be. Simplicity of the language surface
outranks footprint, and that trade is taken knowingly.

**Declined:**
- **A stackless transform of Novis functions.** It would shrink a task to a few hundred bytes, which
  is how async languages reach their concurrency counts, but it colours every function that can
  suspend, and the colour reaches the language surface: a `Core` member that reads a socket would
  need a form ordinary code cannot call.

<sub>See also [`concurrency/try-the-syscall-then-park`](concurrency.md#concurrency-try-the-syscall-then-park), [`concurrency/a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled"></a>

## A task's stack is 1 MiB of reserved address space, resident only where it is touched, and pooled per worker

`rule:concurrency/a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled`

A task's stack is 1 MiB of **reserved** address space with a guard page. Reserved is not committed:
a page a task never touches is never resident on any of the three platforms, so a shallow handler
costs the handful of pages its frames actually wrote. A hundred thousand concurrent tasks is 100 GiB
of address space — unremarkable in a 64-bit process — against a resident cost measured in what the
handlers touched.

The reservation is charged to the request that owns the task, and it is the *reservation* that enters
a worker's admission arithmetic, because address space is the resource an admission decision can count
ahead of time. Resident growth is bounded by the recursion limit that already bounds how deep a task
may go ([`concurrency/a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack)).

Stacks are pooled per worker. A stack is an `mmap` or `VirtualAlloc` pair, which is the wrong thing
to do per request on a hot path, so a freed stack goes back to the pool and is handed to the next
task. The pool never holds more stacks than the worker has had tasks in flight at once. A serving
core also keeps at most its share of `[server] max_in_flight` idle, the number divided by the worker
count and rounded up, read each time a stack comes back so a reload moves it. A stack freed past that
is handed back to the operating system, so one burst does not leave its stacks resident for the life
of the worker. That is the O(in-flight) shape [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority) asks for.

A worker keeps **one pool per role**: the server's own work, such as the accept loop and a
connection, takes from one, and compiled Novis code, an isolate's task and every task beneath it,
from the other. A pooled stack keeps the pages its deepest task touched, so one pool let a connection
keep the pages a program grew. Each pool has the cap above, so a serving core holds up to twice its
share idle, which is one connection stack and one program stack per request in flight.

**An idle core gives the pages back.** When a core is about to wait with nothing ready and has taken
no stack for a whole second, each idle stack returned since the last trim gives back all but its top
8 KiB, through `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` on Unix and `DiscardVirtualMemory` on Windows. The stack
keeps its mapping and its place in the pool. A trim never runs when a stack comes back, which would
be a system call per request, and never while the core keeps taking stacks. It costs one system call
per idle stack on Unix and a few on Windows, once per quiet period, and up to two wakes of a quiet
core. A trim is not a scrubbing guarantee, and on macOS the old bytes may stay: Novis code cannot
read them because the language is memory-safe.

A scheduler that is not a serving core, such as `nvs run`'s or a queue worker's, has no admission
number and keeps its high-water mark. Its tasks are already bounded by `max_tasks` per program, and
`nvs run`'s scheduler ends with its one program, so a second compiled-in number would bound nothing
the work does not.

A parse whose native recursion depth is set by its input, such as `Core\Json::decode` at its 1024-level
ceiling, runs on the worker thread's one **spare stack**, 8 MiB reserved, and never on the task's
own. What is left of a task's stack depends on how deep the program already is and on the build's frame
sizes, so the task's stack cannot promise room for such a parse. The spare stack is one reservation per
worker thread, O(workers), and the pages the deepest parse touched stay resident for the life of the
thread. Code on it never calls compiled Novis code, whose recursion limit is armed for the task's stack.

- **Memory:** each task in flight reserves 1 MiB of address space, charged to its request, and keeps
  resident only the pages its frames touched. So a request whose memory limit is 256 MB runs at most
  about 250 tasks at once. A serving core also holds up to twice its share of
  `max_in_flight` in idle reservations between tasks, with all but 8 KiB of each given back once the
  core is idle, and each worker thread one 8 MiB spare stack.

**Declined:**
- **One stack per request, shared by its connection and its program.** A request can outlive its
  connection: the server still watches its wall time after the peer is gone, so the program needs a
  task, and a stack, of its own.

<sub>See also [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority), [`concurrency/a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack), [`concurrency/a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-stream-is-an-ordinary-io-stream).</sub>

<a id="concurrency-a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack"></a>

## A task's recursion limit is armed from the real bounds of the stack it was handed

`rule:concurrency/a-tasks-recursion-limit-comes-from-its-own-stack`

A task's recursion limit is armed from the base and length of the stack it was actually handed, not
asserted from a compiled-in ceiling. The host allocated that stack and knows its bounds exactly, so
the limit it arms is a fact about the memory the task is standing on.

That is what makes deep recursion inside a task a thrown, catchable error rather than a walk into a
guard page. The width of the stack is set by the same arithmetic: an unwinding reserve already sits
between the soft recursion limit and the hard floor ([`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit)), so a stack has to be
several times that reserve before the two numbers are coherent — which is why a 64 KiB stack is
rejected on arithmetic rather than on taste.

<sub>See also [`errors/on-limit`](errors.md#errors-on-limit), [`concurrency/a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled`](concurrency.md#concurrency-a-task-stack-is-reserved-wide-and-pooled).</sub>
